results.content: Employee Incentive Schemes – What are they? An employee incentive scheme refers to payments or other benefits that an employer may provide to an employee that are in addition to the employee’s base remuneration. Examples of employee incentive payments include:. Performance-based incentives refer to incentives that are provided by an employer after an employee achieves a certain performance target. Generally, an employee will become entitled to, or eligible for, a benefit under an employee incentive scheme because of an agreement between the employee and their employer. This agreement could be part of the employee’s contract of employment or the parties could agree to it separately. It is quite common for an employer to qualify an incentive in an agreement as being provided at the discretion of the employer. 1. Title: Incentive Schemes: Need and Factors | Cost Accounting
# Incentive Schemes: Need and Factors | Cost Accounting. **In this article we will discuss about Incentive Schemes. After reading this article you will learn about: 1. **Need for Incentive Schemes 2. **Factors for Selecting Successful Incentive Schemes.******. #### **Need for Incentive Schemes****:**. It is true that low wages do not necessarily mean low costs, again, higher wages also need not necessarily mean a high wage cost per unit. In fact, it is widely recognised that efficiently organised manufacturing concerns may pay the highest wages, and yet have lowest labour cost. **Incentive schemes are necessary for the following reasons:**. (i) To induce the employees to earn more by producing more. (ii) To reduce cost of production per unit by increasing production. (iii) To reduce production time, which increases efficiency of a worker. (iv) To provide better standard of living of employees by allowing more scope of earning. (v) To enhance the economic condition of a country by increasing per-capita income of the workers. #### **Factors for Selecting Successful Incentive Schemes****:**. **For selecting a successful incentive scheme the following factors should be considered:**. The ultimate aim of an organisation is to increase productivity. Hence, the incentive plan should be such that it can increase productivity. The incentive scheme should be such that it has no adverse effect on the workers. Any adverse effect may increase labour turnover which means increase in cost of production. A good incentive plan will attract efficient workers from outside as also retain those who are already in employment. Due to increase of production, fixed cost are allocated over a greater number of units, resulting in lesser share of overhead cost per unit. Hence, increased volume of production means lower unit fixed cost. **(e)** **Quantity and Quality of output:**. When quantity of production is more important than quality, the method of remuneration should be such as to encourage increased production. On the other hand, if quality is more important than the quantity produced, wage payment should be based preferably on time. ### Related Articles:. 1.
